text:
Africa is getting better at mapping climate risk. The harder problem is making those maps change budgets, projects and operating decisions.

A new OECD, Global Green Growth Institute and World Bank assessment covering 28 African countries finds that hot days have nearly doubled in frequency since the 1990s, while extreme precipitation has increased by more than 150 per cent.

In West Africa, under a very-high-emissions scenario, 2,964 urban settlements could experience more than 180 days a year above 35°C around mid-century.

Those numbers matter because much of Africa's future urban fabric has not yet been built. Roads, substations, markets, schools, clinics and housing designed now may still be operating when those conditions arrive.

But a hazard map does not reduce risk by itself.

A city can know where heat is worst and still have no named institution responsible for changing market shade, school design, working hours, drainage, public-health protocols or substation cooling. A finance ministry can tag climate spending without being able to show whether the money changed exposure or service reliability.

StoneComms' conclusion is that climate data should be treated as decision infrastructure.

We propose a Decision-Ready Climate Record with seven linked fields:

PLACE — where is the decision unit?
THRESHOLD — what physical condition triggers action?
PEOPLE AND SERVICE — who or what is exposed, and what must keep working?
DECISION — what binding choice needs to change?
OWNER — who has authority and operating responsibility?
FINANCE — what pays for preparation, capital and operation?
RESULT — what evidence will show whether it worked?

The aim is not another reporting system. It is to stop climate evidence losing resolution as it moves from science into institutions.

Freetown shows why this matters. The city has translated heat risk into physical market interventions, including shade and solar lighting. Kenya's locally led climate programme has connected participatory risk assessments to county plans and resilience grants.

The finance gap makes this discipline more important. Global Center on Adaptation and Climate Policy Initiative analysis estimates Africa needs at least US$70 billion a year for adaptation, while tracked flows reached US$14.8 billion in 2023.

When capital is scarce, the question cannot simply be whether a project is climate-related. It has to be: what risk is being reduced, for whom, through which service, by which institution, and how will we know?

The most useful climate map is the one that changes what gets built, funded or operated differently.
